content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents FFCV, a framework to eliminate data stalls in the frontend stage of DNN training pipeline. The key components of FCCV include efficient file storage format (.beton), process-level caching, data pre-loading (partly in raw, decompressed format), asynchronous data transfers, and just-in-time compilation using Numba/LLVM. For ResNet-18/50 FFCV demonstrates substantial training throughput gains without losing accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

* Reducing data stalls is important to balance the DNN training pipeline.

* Combining multiple techniques in a single unified framework demonstrates decent speedups.

**Weaknesses**

* As the authors admit at the end, FFCV is effective only for a relative narrow set of DNNs and/or execution environments for which data loading is the bottleneck.

* The performance gains over NVIDIA DALI is pretty marginal.

* Discussion of JPEG hardware-accelerated decoding on A100 is missing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is mostly well written, but some aspects of the framework are not clear. Overall, FFCV combines multiple techniques (i.e., format optimization, caching, dynamic code optimization), which are already explored in other works.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As the authors point out, the DNN pipeline is often not well balanced, and the frontend stage becomes a bottleneck. They take a holistic approach to tackling this problem to propose FFCV, which can replace a popular data loader like PyTorch data loader. While the framework might be practically useful, the techniques introduced in FFCV are more or less known to reduce the degree of pipeline imbalance. The only part that was relatively new to me is just-in-time compilation of the image processing pipeline using Numba/LLVM, which seems pretty useful. However, I feel the impact of this work would be marginal for the following reasons.

FFCV mainly targets the model training for image classification like ImageNet, and JPEG-encoded images are lesser of a bottleneck. It's because (i) the image format has high compression ratio (i.e., I/O is not a bottleneck) and (ii) JPEG decoding is usually accelerated by either GPU or specialized hardware (e.g., NVIDIA A100 GPU has a custom hardware accelerator for JPEG decoding). What is not clear about this work is how JPEG decoding is performed. They should have used the custom hardware on A100 or a GPU-optimized implementation of *nvjpeg* at the very least.  According to our own evaluation, JPEG decoding is seldom a bottleneck on modern GPUs, and I suspect the authors' claim of the JPEG decoder being the bottleneck is somewhat exaggerated.

Another concern is the availability of NVIDIA DALI.  DALI does not require special hardware support and is readily available on mainstream GPUs such as V100 and later generations. The throughput advantage of FFCV over DALI is only marginal at best, and it is hard to justify the cost of this somewhat intrusive software changes to the DNN training pipeline. If we use DALI, pretty much all the downstream stages after data reading happen on GPU to eliminate this frotend bottleneck for the most part.

Finally, as the authors admit in the conclusion section, FFCV is effective only for a relatively small model and/or relatively weak compute capabitlities of the host.  It would not be effective for large models (for which gradient computation on GPU dominates the pipeline time) or where data is fast to load and process (e.g., like JPEG images). A recent work [Bae, ECCV 2022] shows that lossless image format like PNG has more of a data processing bottleneck, which might be a better target for FFCV. However, the proposed framework in its current form looks somewhat overfit to a specific workload and hardware configurations.

[Bae, ECCV 2022] [L3: Accelerator-Friendly Lossless Image Format for High-Resolution, High-Throughput DNN Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.08711)

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a framework, FFCV, for increasing the DL training throughput by reducing the data loading and processing overheads. FFCV combines a preprocessing phase, that transforms the data into a format suitable for high-throughput loading, and a loading phase, that loads data from DRAM during the training phase. By introducing a custom file-format, that addresses some of the limitations of existing data loaders, and several runtime processing improvements, such as JIT compiling the data processing pipeline using Numba, FFCV is able to achieve significant speedups over the default pytorch dataloaders for the ImageNet training dataset. These performance improvements also generalize to other modalities outside of image processing datasets as well.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
--------------------
- The authors provide a good description of not only how their proposed data format works but also the underlying issues that motivated their design decisions.
- The performance improvement over the baseline PyTorch dataloader for the ImageNet examples they provided is impressive and supports the assertion that data processing and loading are the key limiters to training performance.
- The multi-model training examples are quite interesting and demonstrate the utility of a faster data processing pipeline to train multiple models in parallel.
- The proposed file-format sets itself apart from alternatives used for Webdataset, TFRecord, and RecordIO in regards to searchability and indexing examples.

Weaknesses:
----------------------
- The major weakness, and the main question almost any researcher in the community will ask, regards differentiating FFCV from the DALI, which appears to be its only true competitor. The performance improvements of FFCV over DALI, in all tests, are marginal so it is not clear how impactful the differences between the packages manifest during training.
- It wasn't mentioned in section 4.4 if DALI was applicable to the sparse linear regression problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The clarity and quality of the writing in the main portion of the paper are reasonable. However, the writing in the Appendix needs more work to improve the quality of the wording.

- The authors do a reasonable job describing the novelty of their implementation, however, in the end the performance seems to be inline with existing alternate solutions which, somewhat minimizes the overall impact.

- I'm confident the results are reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall this paper is well-motivated and provides ample support for the author's claims regarding the importance of the data processing pipeline on performance during training. The major weakness of the result is the availability of a competing solution that delivers a similar performance so it is not clear where the advantages lie.

I believe if the authors are able to provide more support in section 4.4 regarding the lack of DALI support for a wide range of modalities outside of image processing this would improve the novelty claims and contributions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new data loading system to improve I/O and pre-processing speed. Their solution includes a performance-tailored file format, additional loading and caching support, and a JIT compilation support for user-defined pre-processing code. They report training times on ResNet against the pytorch loader and nvidia DALI.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- The authors take a broad view of the data handling problem, and they investigate and attack the problem from a variety of angles. This is refreshing, as it keeps the various challenges and solutions in context.

- The authors make a concerted effort to succinctly capture the takeaways and key points from each of the topics they look at. This helps keep important concepts in the reader's mind, and it makes the paper more accessible to a broader audience.

- I appreciated the acknowledgement of qualitative differences in memory capacity of training platforms. Often, papers make restrictive assumptions about whether something 'fits' or not, whereas the authors here clearly enumerate disinct scenarios (S4) which help show off why some of the complexity in the earlier parts of the paper is needed.

**Weaknesses:**
- The chosen baselines seemed a bit cherry-picked. The authors even mention other SOTA work in this area (e.g., Mohan et al.) in their related works but choose to evaluate against different (and weaker) baselines. It seems like the authors are trying to showcase their performance over known-unoptimal Python code, which---while widespread---isn't really the competition here. In point of fact, the depth of the bottleneck analysis in the referenced work tends to be better than this paper.

- The choice to use only a single model and dataset skews the results somewhat. While I agree with the authors that loading and pre-processing is a widespread challenge, it affects different models and datasets quite differently, and the lack of diversity hurts the authors' claims about the generality, flexibility, and adaptibility of their proposed system.

- I was surprised to see little talk of underlying I/O hardware. Feeding data from local disk, local NVRAM, distributed storage, or streamed from the network all would seem to require different treatment, but the authors only mention some of these factors in passing.

- The paper really missed a breakdown of the contribution of the various performance enhancements. The authors paint a picture of a multi-faceted challenge, but their results speak only of aggregates. This is especially acute given their own observations about where time is spent (Fig 2). If 90% of the speedup is coming from only one optimization (JIT for preprocessing, for example), then it's a bit disingenuous to imply the full proposal is necessary.

- Perhaps this is subjective, but I felt this topic deserved a lot more depth and scrutiny that might come from being discussed in a systems venue. While the application under study is clearly relevant to this audience, it seems like the authors are not diving particularly deeply into the challenges of the problem they are facing, nor is the efficacy of their solution investigated particularly well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:**
The writing flowed fairly well, and the authors' tone was engaging and helpful in guiding the reader along. However, the level of detail was uneven---some places seemed almost overly thorough (e.g., the `.beton` description), where others were left vague (e.g., SSD vs. HDD optimization; preprocessing pipeline used).

**Quality:**
Optimizations are generally described well in the paper, and the motivations and high-leve intuitions provided seem solid. There are some places where the authors oversimplify, but for the most part, the authors can be forgiven, as it is a lot of ground to cover for a very diverse audience. That said, some claims remain more or less unevaluated in the paper (e.g., subsetting/indexing support for `.beton`, preprocessing op grouping/fusion prevalence), which is less excusable. Ultimately, the analysis and experimentation that is done in the paper is less problematic than that which was avoided.

**Novelty:**
While some of the components the authors introduce are perhaps not unique (e.g., accelerating Python codes through Numba, exploiting local caching or better use of OS caches), it seems to me the contribution of the paper comes from the integration and extension of several techniques to solve a complex problem. That said, there *are* questions about the novelty with respect to other work that does similar things. One solution to this would be to showcase where gains are coming from. If the benefits of FFCV are localized to pieces that are unique, then the novelty of the paper improves. Since it isn't described, however, we cannot know.

**Reproducibility:**
For the most part, details of the experimental setup were presented well, but I was left with a lot of questions about the actual implementations used. The 'implementation held constant' (S4.1, p8, par2) comment, for instance, clarified little since we didn't really get much clarity on the 'implementation' to begin with . Is Fig 4 an accurate reflection of the pre-processing pipeline used in the evaluation of Fig 1 and Fig 5?
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors tackle an important problem with a refreshingly encompassing solution, but the paper is hampered by insufficient quantitative analysis and weak evaluation choices.

content.title: FFCV: Accelerating Training by Removing Data Bottlenecks
content.TL;DR: We present FFCV, an easy-to-use yet highly optimized library for training machine learning models.
content.abstract: We present FFCV, a library for easy, fast, resource-efficient training of machine learning models. FFCV speeds up model training by eliminating (often subtle) data bottlenecks from the training process. In particular, we combine techniques such as an efficient file storage format, caching, data pre-loading, asynchronous data transfer, and just-in-time compilation to (a) make data loading and transfer significantly more efficient, ensuring that GPUs can reach full utilization; and (b) offload as much data processing as possible to the CPU asynchronously, freeing GPU up capacity for training. Using FFCV, we train ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on the ImageNet dataset with a state-of-the-art tradeoff between accuracy and training time. For example, across the range of ResNet-50 models we test, we obtain the same accuracy as the best baselines in half the time. We demonstrate FFCV's performance, ease-of-use, extensibility, and ability to adapt to resource constraints through several case studies.
